name: Rural-to-urban Migration
description: Movement from villages to towns and cities helped reshape Iran’s settlement geography, but it is only one component of urbanization. Historical comparisons require attention to war displacement, settlement reclassification, and the increasing importance of moves between urban places.

seo.title: Rural-to-urban Migration in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore village-to-city migration in Iran, its changing historical importance, and the limits of census evidence.

content.heading: A movement of people—and a question of classification
content.content:
Rural-to-urban migration means changing residence from a rural settlement to an urban one. It should be distinguished from a village becoming administratively urban while its residents remain in place. Encyclopaedia Iranica identifies both changes in settlement definitions and the absorption of villages into expanding cities as important complications in Iran’s historical statistics. An increase in the urban population therefore cannot, by itself, establish how many people moved from villages. [s1]

The distinction also changes how a landscape is read. A settlement near an expanding city may acquire an urban classification without a corresponding departure of its established population. Conversely, a household can leave a village for a small town rather than a major metropolitan centre. The meaningful comparison is between documented origins and destinations, using the classifications applicable to the reporting period. [s1]

content.heading: From a dominant narrative to one stream among several
content.content:
Iran’s rural-to-urban history includes forced displacement as well as movement associated with changing livelihoods. The historical account in Encyclopaedia Iranica emphasizes the Iran–Iraq War: people fled occupied villages, while postwar return movements followed a different timetable because damaged settlements were not always ready to receive residents. These circumstances make a simple story of uninterrupted movement toward cities misleading. [s1]

Later evidence shows a migration system increasingly dominated by movement between urban places. A KNOMAD report reproduces a UNFPA table in which rural-to-urban moves account for a smaller share of internal migration in the later reporting intervals than in the earliest interval shown. These are shares of recorded migration, not annual probabilities that a rural resident will leave. The unequal interval lengths also prevent interpreting them as directly comparable annual volumes. [s2]

content.title: Rural-to-urban share of internal migration by reporting interval

content.heading: What the evidence can establish
content.content:
The table describes the composition of migration rather than the scale of rural population loss. A falling share can coexist with substantial movement, and a national percentage does not identify which villages are losing residents. Interpretation also requires separating migration from other components of population change. [s2]

For international readers, the useful conclusion is that village-to-city movement remains a distinct subject within Iran’s migration history, while urbanization is a broader demographic and administrative process. Treating the two as interchangeable obscures both the experiences of migrants and the changing boundaries of the settlements they leave or enter. [s1][s2]

name: Interprovincial Migration
description: Interprovincial migration redistributes residents across Iran’s provincial boundaries. Research connects its geography with unequal opportunities and environmental conditions, while showing why net migration alone cannot describe all movement.

seo.title: Interprovincial Migration in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand migration across Iran’s provincial boundaries, regional inequalities, environmental research, and census limitations.

content.heading: Crossing a provincial boundary
content.content:
Interprovincial migration classifies a residential move by its administrative geography. It differs from rural-to-urban migration, which classifies the settlements at either end. A move can belong to both categories, but crossing a provincial boundary does not necessarily mean leaving a village for a city. Iranian migration research distinguishes recent migration, previous residence, and lifetime migration; these measures answer different questions and should not be combined without checking their definitions. [s1]

Two further distinctions help readers interpret provincial comparisons. In-migration counts arrivals and outmigration counts departures. Net migration subtracts departures from arrivals, whereas gross movement includes both directions. A small net balance can therefore conceal considerable movement. The national synthesis by Sadeghi and colleagues describes limited population redistribution despite ongoing mobility, illustrating why migration activity and its net demographic effect require separate attention. [s1]

content.heading: A geography of unequal opportunities
content.content:
The published abstract of that synthesis identifies net population gains in central provinces around Tehran and losses toward eastern and western peripheral areas. It links this geography to socioeconomic inequalities. This is a broad interpretation of census-era patterns, rather than a claim that every province within those regions behaves identically or that the same destinations remain dominant today. [s1]

For a reader comparing places, a provincial balance is best treated as an entry point. It does not identify every origin–destination connection, distinguish household members’ individual motives, or establish whether a move was permanent. Those questions require more detailed migration histories than an aggregate balance provides.

content.heading: Environmental pressures alongside economic conditions
content.content:
Farzanegan, Gholipour, and Javadian examined migration and air pollution using census observations and satellite measurements. Their models associate greater aerosol pollution with higher net outmigration and stronger economic activity with lower net outmigration. The study supports considering environmental quality alongside economic opportunity; it does not establish pollution as the motive of every household that moved. [s2]

Its geography needs particular care. The dependent variable uses departures minus arrivals in selected major cities within each province, divided by their combined population. That is a net-outmigration measure, whose positive direction differs from a conventional net-inmigration balance. It is also not a complete census of all moves between provincial boundaries. Provincial labels on a research result must therefore be read together with the actual population covered. [s2]

The practical lesson is to ask what a map measures before interpreting its colours: arrivals, departures, a net balance, or a population-normalized rate. Evidence for an environmental relationship can enrich the explanation of regional migration without replacing those basic distinctions. [s2]

name: Skilled Migration
description: Skilled migration from Iran includes the international movement of researchers, professionals, and other workers with specialized education or expertise. Its significance depends on how skills are defined, whether departures are temporary or lasting, and what connections migrants maintain with Iran.

seo.title: Skilled Migration from Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore skilled migration from Iran, the evidence on professional and scientific mobility, and the limits of brain-drain estimates.

content.heading: Who counts as a skilled migrant?
content.content:
Skilled migration is not a single statistical category. Education-based accounts identify degree holders; professional accounts focus on occupations; scientific-mobility studies track researchers. These approaches overlap without describing identical populations. OECD country profiles, for example, distinguish educational attainment and highly educated emigration, while scientific-mobility research uses publication affiliations. A figure about researchers cannot automatically stand for all skilled workers. [s1][s4]

The distinction between a stock and a flow is equally important. A population of skilled people living abroad accumulates over time; it is not the number leaving in a particular year. Nor does an overseas affiliation necessarily establish permanent settlement. These distinctions are essential when reading research on Iran’s internationally mobile professionals. [s2][s4]

content.heading: Careers, institutions, and the decision to leave
content.content:
The Stanford Iran 2040 working paper interprets skilled emigration through interacting economic, political, and social conditions. Its framework distinguishes long-running pressures from particular triggers and from networks that help people move. This is an analytical account, not a survey establishing one motive shared by every emigrant. [s2]

A Migration Policy Institute article likewise discusses research opportunities, career prospects, restrictions affecting academics, sanctions, and economic deterioration. It also includes health professionals in the discussion, showing why the subject extends beyond universities. These accounts describe the circumstances examined at publication; they do not provide a verified inventory of professional departures near the editorial cutoff. [s3]

content.heading: What scientific mobility can reveal
content.content:
The Stanford study combines migration statistics with an algorithm identifying scholars of Iranian descent in publication records. Its scholar population should therefore be distinguished from a register of Iranian-born people who recently departed. Descent, birthplace, employment location, and migration date are different attributes. [s2]

A separate study of scientific mobility in the Middle East and North Africa uses affiliations recorded in publications to examine movement and international collaboration. This approach makes cross-border research connections visible, but its evidence concerns publishing scholars. It cannot establish the movements of professionals who do not publish, and a collaboration link should not be interpreted as a residential move. [s4]

content.heading: Loss of expertise and continuing connections
content.content:
“Brain drain” describes concern about the loss of expertise available to institutions and employers at home. The Stanford paper also discusses potential diaspora contributions, including collaboration, investment, and temporary or lasting return. These are possible channels of contribution rather than proof that departures have been offset. [s2]

An assessment of Iran therefore needs several questions rather than one headline total: which skills are leaving, which institutions face shortages, how long migrants remain abroad, and what professional connections continue. Existing research establishes the importance of the subject, while differences in definitions limit comparisons between estimates. A defensible account keeps those populations and measurement methods visible. [s1][s2][s4]
